angleRead.name: Trevor Shimizu
angleRead.text: Standing on the 12th Street platform at 7:40 on a clear morning, watching the weekend crowd trickle in instead of surge. The numbers tell a story of a city that stayed home — every station down, every corridor lighter. But the interesting part isn't the drop. It's that 12th Street fell hardest, and 19th Street held its on-time rate up while ridership fell nearly as much. The weekend rule explains the baseline, but the rows carry their own reasons: game days, events, the Baylight construction vote. I want to talk to the people who work the system — the station manager who sees the platforms empty, the operators who run the trains through it. What does a quiet weekend on the line feel like fro

plan.focus: The weekend ridership drop across all eight stations, with 12th Street leading the decline, and what transit workers observe when the system runs light.
plan.why: The citywide pattern is clear — weekend rule, clear weather, everyone down. But the human layer is what's missing from the ledger: the workers who staff a system when the riders don't come, and what they see from their posts.

plan.interpretation: The weekend frame explains the broad drop, but the station rows carry their own texture — game days and events that didn't lift ridership the way they might on a weekday, construction that may have pushed riders away, and a system that ran on time at some stations while slipping at others. The pattern suggests a city that chose not to move this weekend, and the workers who showed up anyway are the ones who can say what that looked like.
